title: Japanese-tit call order: evidence and interpretations
review_depth: Direct publisher full text reviewed for the 2016 primary paper (Methods, Experiments 1–2, Results, figures and ethics) and 2022 follow-up (selected Methods, Results, ethics, data/code statements and rights). The linked 2022 Figshare v1 tables were checked against the current official API sizes and MD5 values, paired on trial metadata, and summarized with the project standard-library script; the deposited R scripts were read as text, not executed. For the 2017 paper, publisher-indexed primary text exposed the abstract, selected Results, STAR Methods, statistics and data statement; its direct ScienceDirect page returned HTTP 403. The 2017 Mendeley Data v1 landing metadata and record-level license were reviewed, but its files were not. For Schlenker et al. (2024), the main text (Sections I–VII) of the official HAL v1 author-accepted manuscript was reviewed; the formal appendices were inspected selectively, not recalculated. The separate Wiley supporting-information PDF returned HTTP 403 and was not reviewed. Beckers et al. (2024) Sections 1–4 were read in the full text available through PubMed Central; its conceptual critique is not a new animal experiment. For the adjacent Coye & Dutour (2025) study (source 268), publisher-indexed Methods, Results and Discussion passages and the University of Western Australia repository abstract/access record were reviewed; direct ScienceDirect retrieval returned HTTP 403, so the full article file, figures, supplement and complete statistical details were not reviewed. No inferential model was reproduced and no independent Talk2Nature specialist review has occurred.
seo_description: Japanese-tit playback studies test call order and source. Their receiver responses are documented; the interpretation as syntax remains debated.
finding: Japanese great tits showed different receiver behaviors under component calls, natural versus reversed order, and single- versus two-source playback; a bounded novel cross-species sequence also elicited stronger responses than its reversal, while a matched ABC–zi control was weak. In the 2022 deposited binary table, the natural single-source 1A-R condition had an approach event in 13/16 flock trials and wing-flicking in 15/16; the other three treatments had approach events in 2–3/16 and wing-flicking in 1–4/16. These aggregate counts reproduce the descriptive pattern only. They do not establish a unique mechanism: one published critique agrees that receiver behavior is sensitive to order and source but disputes that this demonstrates Core-Merge or hierarchical syntax.
limitations: These are species-, population- and task-bounded receiver-response results, not general animal-language or translation evidence. The 2017 novelty test combined a familiar heterospecific call type with Japanese-tit calls; it does not establish open-ended productivity, and its comparison with ABC–D used earlier data from another year. The 2022 study extends the same research line in the same species, not an independent replication. Its two Figshare v1 outcome tables contain no audio and no location fields; dates and caller_ID fields remain in ignored local files. The current official Figshare API reports MD5 values and the two received data tables match them; this confirms byte agreement with the current provider manifest, not scientific validity or a data-to-figure reproduction. The committed summary contains aggregates only. Its script does not run the deposited R code or reproduce mixed-effects models and adjusted contrasts. Schlenker et al. (2024) offer two formal accounts that fit the source-separation result under different assumptions. Beckers et al. (2024) agree the evidence shows sensitivity to call order and distinguishable responses to 1AR versus 2AR, but argue that the experiment does not establish Core-Merge or hierarchical syntax; a finite-list account fits the 2022 result, and a finite-state/concatenation account is proposed for the broader order pattern. This is a published interpretive disagreement, not a new empirical result or consensus. The 2025 Carolina-wren/great-tit study is adjacent cross-family receiver-response evidence; it did not reverse order and is not a test or replication of Japanese-tit sequence-order sensitivity. No Talk2Nature playback or animal-facing experiment is proposed.
lesson: Report the measured receiver behavior and separate it from the theoretical label placed on the behavior. The 2022 source tables descriptively show a large difference between one natural same-source condition and the other tested conditions, but do not choose among Core-Merge, finite-list, concatenation or other mechanisms. A useful next review should assess the 2017 cross-species result alongside the 2016 and 2022 controls, and distinguish linear order, source linkage and hierarchical generalization. Any animal-facing study requires qualified scientific and welfare oversight; these results do not support an AI-generated verbal translation.
next_review: Invite an independent comparative-communication specialist to assess the published interpretations, including the Beckers et al. critique, Schlenker et al. alternatives, the 2017 cross-species sequence and the limits of the 2025 comparator. Before any inferential reanalysis, define a data-to-table mapping, obtain an independently checked analysis plan and freeze the software environment; the current project script is descriptive only. Seek the 2017 Mendeley file inventory and exact file terms only through an authorized route. Any animal study requires approval by the responsible scientific team.

study_snapshot: 2016: 21 adult birds in the component experiment; 34 different birds in the order experiment (17 per treatment).
2016 component experiment: ABC, D, ABC–D and matched background control; call treatments used matched exemplars and randomized order.
2016 order test: natural ABC–D versus reversed D–ABC, with call exemplars and interval features balanced; one treatment per bird.
2017: 56 birds, 14 per condition; ABC–tää responses were stronger than tää–ABC, while ABC–zi and zi–ABC responses were both weak and similar.
2017 follow-up: 42 flocks, 14 per call type; D, tää and shortened-tää playbacks tested call category and acoustic-similarity alternatives.
2022 follow-up: 64 flocks, 16 per condition; one/two speakers crossed with natural/reversed order, with a shrike model present.

The Figshare v1 deposit has two paired 64-row behavioral outcome tables and two R scripts. A standard-library audit matched the table trial metadata and binary/count outcomes; the single-source natural 1A-R group had approach in 13/16 flocks and wing-flicking in 15/16. This is descriptive only; no mixed model or deposited code was run. No audio is present.

Coye & Dutour: 96 great tits, six treatments, 16 per treatment; approach did not differ among call treatments, while wing-flicking was more frequent after complete Carolina-wren or great-tit FME–D sequences than after D calls or controls. No reversed-order condition was tested.

Beckers et al. agree the experiments show order sensitivity and different responses to one-source versus two-source AR, but argue this does not establish Core-Merge or hierarchy; finite-list and finite-state/concatenation alternatives remain.
Horizontal scanning, approach and wing-flicking displays, not an AI-generated verbal interpretation. The 2024 theory papers add alternative explanations but no new playback result.

theory_comparison.intro: Schlenker et al. (2024) compare Minimal Compositionality and Bird Implicatures for ABC–D. Beckers et al. (2024) challenge the Core-Merge interpretation and discuss finite-list and concatenation-based finite-state accounts. These are published interpretations of prior receiver behavior, not competing trained models or new experiments.

items.name: Minimal Compositionality
items.account: ABC–D combines the call meanings under one existential claim: the same noteworthy event licenses both alert and recruitment. Separate ABC and D utterances make two claims, which need not refer to the same event.
items.prediction: Separate calls can still support mobbing if receivers can link both to the same threat, but the link should be harder than for a single ABC–D sequence.
items.assumption: D alone must carry an event-like, existential meaning. The authors note that this is not established by the cited approach response.

items.name: Bird Implicatures
items.account: ABC–D is treated as a more informative alternative to ABC and/or D. A standalone call can imply that the fuller ABC–D combination is false, which can block a mobbing response even if the calls are understood as separate utterances.
items.prediction: Source-separated ABC and D should tend toward a non-mobbing inference; this account does not require D alone to refer to a noteworthy event.
items.assumption: The analysis needs ABC–D to be evoked as an alternative. The authors favor a receiver-centered version to handle the hybrid ABC–D* result.

items.name: Finite-list and finite-state/concatenation alternatives (Beckers et al., 2024)
items.account: A finite-list explanation treats A, R and the natural AR call as distinct complex vocalization types and can fit the 2022 treatment pattern without inferring a productive combinatorial operation. To accommodate order sensitivity across the 2016, 2017 and 2022 studies, the authors suggest a finite-state account based on ordered call bigrams.
items.prediction: The cited results can show learned sensitivity to call identity, linear order and source while leaving hierarchical structure and open-ended productivity unestablished.
items.assumption: The critique is a conceptual analysis, not a new experiment or quantitative reanalysis. Its finite-list and finite-state explanations are alternatives to the interpretation, not directly tested models.

theory_comparison.takeaway: The 2022 result supports a bounded receiver-response difference between one-source natural AR and the other tested conditions. It does not uniquely establish Core-Merge, recursion or general language syntax. Schlenker et al. offer two formal accounts; Beckers et al. accept order sensitivity but argue finite-list or concatenation-based accounts can explain the evidence. The 2017 cross-species result remains a point any unified account must address.

questions: Which 2016 and 2017 contrasts best support an order-sensitive receiver response, and what alternatives remain after the reported component, reversal, novelty and call-type controls?
What does the 2022 one/two-speaker comparison establish about source linkage, and what does it leave open about mechanism or independent replication?

How should the 2025 Carolina-wren/great-tit study affect cross-species generalization? Its sequence-versus-D-only comparison did not reverse order, so what does it add about receiver response, and what does it leave open about order or meaning?

title: NatureLM-audio: a bioacoustic model, not a nature translator
review_depth: Reviewed the ICLR 2025 proceedings abstract, architecture/training sections, BEANS-Zero tasks and evaluation, Tables 3–6, the BirdNET/Perch comparison caveat, conclusion and risk discussion. Reviewed Sections 2–4 and limitations of the 11-page arXiv v2 follow-up identified by its authors as a NeurIPS 2025 workshop paper. Checked the official overview/Quick Start, the Hugging Face model and dataset metadata, and the official code/data repository inventories and license files described in the source records. No dataset files, code or model weights were acquired, no inference was run and no results were reproduced. On October 13, also reviewed the BEANS-Zero dataset card at its visible commit, its live file inventory, and the official evaluation-code repository at pinned main commit 31d4487ee6452ae6c31853d45fd38b7d4150372d, including the project metadata. No dataset shards, sample rows, code or dependencies were downloaded or executed.
finding: NatureLM-audio combines a BEATs audio encoder with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and responds to audio-plus-text prompts with outputs such as species labels, detections, call types, life-stage classes and captions. Its ICLR 2025 paper reports strong results on several BEANS-Zero tasks and evaluates held-out taxa; the paper cautions that BirdNET and Perch comparison datasets overlap their training data, so those are topline rather than fully fair comparisons. A NeurIPS 2025 workshop follow-up preprint exposes prompt-format brittleness: asking for common and scientific names together reduced accuracy to 6–12% on two benchmark components compared with prompts asking for one name. For those combined-name prompts, the authors report that LoRA interpolation at about α=0.7 raises accuracy from 6% to 45% on Watkins and 12% to 63% on CBI. Separately, on one 425-sample, 40-class closed-set unseen-family task, reported F1 rose from 0.09 to 0.28 (the authors describe this as a >200% relative improvement). These are bounded classification and instruction-following results, not evidence that the model discovers what an animal means or can hold a conversation with it. The current training-data viewer lists 26.4 million rows; the paper notes that prompt counts can derive from the same audio, so row counts are not unique recordings. The official BEANS-Zero card reports 91,965 examples in a single test split and says the composite is not intended for commercial use; it documents a license field per sample. The live Hugging Face tree lists 50.5 GB, while the companion GitHub README says about 100 GB for a complete non-streaming download. Its tasks cover classification, detection, call-type/lifestage and captioning, not receiver comprehension or communication meaning.
limitations: The ICLR results are benchmark-specific, and Talk2Nature has not independently reproduced them. The follow-up is a NeurIPS 2025 workshop paper/preprint, not a Talk2Nature validation; its authors state that the unseen-family closed-set result is limited in scope. Current official documentation says the v1.1 demo was updated in April 2026, while its Quick Start says performance is strongest for birds, especially in North America and Western Europe; calls above about 8 kHz (including bat calls) are outside the model frequency range; tropical regions are harder; wrong-taxon prompts are not reliably rejected; and emotion interpretation or translation beyond call-type prediction is unsupported. Several other prompted tasks are explicitly experimental. The model card identifies CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 weights with Llama 3.1 terms also applicable. The 26.4M-row training dataset displays a generic “other” license and its row-level license values differ. BEANS-Zero also has a generic Hub-level “other” value, but its card explicitly says it is a composite, exposes a per-sample license field and is not intended for commercial use. No sample-level rights were inspected. Its live Hub page lists 50.5 GB while its official code README estimates about 100 GB; the size discrepancy is unresolved. The NatureLM code repository and merging-code repository declare MIT, but that does not clear weights or datasets. At the pinned BEANS-Zero code commit, the root inventory has no LICENSE and pyproject.toml declares no license; reuse permission remains unresolved. No files were acquired, and no model or code was run.
lesson: Treat a fluent answer as a model prediction about a defined acoustic task, not as an animal’s message. For Talk2Nature, keep the first software value in passive recording, observation, and transparent researcher review; clearly separate human-entered notes from model guesses. If a later benchmark is justified, select one labelable task, pin model and data versions, compare against simple and context-only baselines, hold out animals or sites where appropriate, test prompt sensitivity, and document each component’s license before any run. The large Llama-based model and its non-commercial weights are not a default phone or paid-product dependency.
next_review: Ask qualified bioacoustic and ML reviewers which single task and holdout unit would answer a useful project question. BEANS-Zero can inform cross-taxon classification/detection/captioning evaluation, but its test-only design, component-specific terms, no-commercial-use notice and unresolved code license make it unsuitable as the first Talk2Nature communication benchmark. Reconcile training and benchmark component rights, pin exact code/model releases, and estimate compute only after a rights-cleared dataset and independent labels exist. Do not start AutoResearch until its documented data, reviewer, split, metric, locked-test, baseline and execution-boundary gates are all met.

title: BEANS-Next and ROOTS: a broad bioacoustics benchmark, not a translation dataset
review_depth: Targeted review of the October 2026 primary preprint: abstract, task taxonomy, data construction, benchmark split description, reported results/limitations, risks and reproducibility statement; also the official project page and Hugging Face cards. Full appendices, individual data rows, source licenses, code and model artifacts were not audited or acquired. No benchmark was run.
finding: BEANS-Next evaluates 45 tasks with 37,718 examples across acoustic perception, biological-category recognition, scene understanding and in-context learning. ROOTS is a separate training resource reported to contain 44 million audio-language pairs from 6.5 million distinct audio clips. The authors describe BEANS-Next evaluation examples as real recordings paired with human- or dataset-provided annotations; text templates and LLMs format the supported annotations into prompts rather than creating new benchmark labels. They state the benchmark audio and derivatives are disjoint from ROOTS and use held-out species where applicable. ROOTS combines curated recordings and structured/free-text metadata with audio-derived information and synthetic audio scenes. The paper reports capability gains after tier-specific fine-tuning, while its overview still identifies weaknesses in open-ended description, counting and transfer to real-world recordings.
limitations: This is a new arXiv preprint; review and reproduction status were not independently established. It benchmarks predictions against annotations, not whether an animal understood a signal or what it meant. ROOTS includes metadata-grounded LLM-generated text and synthetic scenes; those are useful supervision but not additional observed animal conversations. The authors flag taxonomic/geographic bias and possible hallucinated species, behavior or counts. ROOTS' Hugging Face card reports license `other`, and its source audio is not redistributed; each input's rights and provenance need separate review. No resource is admitted to Talk2Nature training or commercial use.
lesson: The useful ML lesson is to broaden supervision beyond species names while keeping each claim tied to the evidence that produced its label. A metadata-generated question can teach a model to retrieve or predict a documented fact; it cannot by itself validate a biological message. For Talk2Nature, use BEANS-Next as a capability map and ROOTS as a methods reference, then test one narrow, source-cleared task with controls and independent biological review.
next_review: Audit the current BEANS-Next and ROOTS component-level data and code terms before any execution. For the project's communication-adjacent study, preserve the separately documented bat context candidate and resolve its specialist, file-join and grouped-evaluation gates; do not substitute a broad audio-language benchmark for receiver-response evidence. Keep AutoResearch NOT READY until the existing admission, reviewer, split, metric and locked-test gates pass.

title: What bark classification can tell us
seo_description: A full methods review of a dog-bark study: dog-held-out context classification predicts associations with induced situations, not what dogs mean.
review_depth: Full seven-page ACL Anthology paper reviewed on 2026-10-13, including Dataset, segmentation/annotation, all four task sections, five results tables and Limitations. No data, code or weights were acquired or executed; no result was reproduced.
finding: The study reports 62.18% accuracy for Wav2Vec2 pretrained on 960 hours of human LibriSpeech, versus a 56.37% majority baseline, on a selected four-class bark/context task. The result is prediction of association with induced study situations, not a test of what dogs understand or mean.
limitations: The 74 dogs were recorded in owners’ homes in Tepic and Puebla during designed exposures such as stranger, play and owner-related situations. Sound segments were manually assigned one of 14 labels from information associated with the stimulus; 8,755 of 16,789 segments are non-dog sounds. The four-class grounding subset mixes vocal form (bark, squeal, grunt) with stranger-related exposure. Dog-held-out folds are reported, but the paper does not describe household, owner, session, stimulus-instance or recording-condition grouping. This is not proof that those groups leaked; their independence cannot be checked from the paper. The paper does not report an independently observer-coded behavior-label stream for these segments or a receiver-response test of the calls. No replication was performed. Results do not establish broad emotion inference, semantics or translation.
lesson: Dog-held-out validation is a useful control for unseen-dog generalization, but it does not by itself show generalization across homes, sessions or stimulus instances. A phone-based passive-observation question would need naturally occurring, independently observed context labels and appropriate group keys; do not transfer this induced-stimulus score to parrots or other species.
next_review: Treat this as a methods comparator. Before any future request for data or baselines, define the exact replication question and verify access, privacy, recording/session/household grouping, label provenance, model checkpoint identity and component rights. No author contact or acquisition has occurred.

title: Giving parrots a choice to connect
seo_description: A nine-parrot study compares live and prerecorded calls; a reversed and transposed table row and caregiver mediation limit interpretation.
review_depth: Published paper pages 3–12 reviewed for participant screening/ethics, protocol, analysis, results and limitations. Page 9 was rendered and Table 2's P1–P9 differences recalculated from the displayed session counts. The current University of Glasgow deposit record and Crossref DOI relation metadata were checked. No raw-data reanalysis or replication.
finding: In a six-month, nine-parrot home study, Table 2 lists 65 parrot-triggered live calls and 40 playback calls out of 108 possible in each phase. Recalculation from the displayed counts gives live-minus-playback differences of +50, +17, +75, +17, +8, -8, -8, +33 and +25 percentage points for P1–P9. The printed row is reversed for seven birds and appears to swap the P3/P5 entries. title: Plant acoustic emissions: detection is not communication
review_depth: Read the main 2023 Cell article and its full STAR Methods, including the recording, preprocessing, model evaluation and results sections; checked the relevant figure legends and selected supporting captions. Read the 2024 Opinion's historical framing, mechanism discussion, receiver-evidence conclusion and open questions. finding: Khait et al. report airborne ultrasonic emissions from stressed tomato and tobacco in an acoustic box and greenhouse, and classify plant condition from recordings. The system used paired CM16 ultrasound microphones per plant at 500 kHz, with a 20 kHz high-pass filter; an event counted as plant-associated only when both microphones aimed at that plant recorded it. The plant-held-out folds reduce leakage from repeated sounds of the same plant, but do not establish generalization to new sites, devices, species or field noise. The later moth study in source 16 supplies a bounded receiver-response result in one moth/plant setting, not evidence of plant intention or a general language. Dryad lists the recordings under its CC0 repository policy, but the archive contents were not inspected; the Zenodo classifier record has no license stated.

finding: In controlled choices, female Egyptian cotton leafworm moths (Spodoptera littoralis) changed where they laid egg clusters when playback of drought-stressed tomato-plant clicks was present. title: Fungal electrical activity: a sensor study, not a decoded language

review_stage: Full primary article and dataset metadata review; supplement and files unreviewed
review_depth: Reviewed the full PMC article text, including Methods, Results and Table 1, figures, Discussion, data statement and article license, plus the Mendeley Data v1 description, displayed license and visible Files section. finding: Buffi et al. tested a printed fungal-potential card on one Fusarium oxysporum strain (NEU 195). Table 1 reports a significant pre-induction power-spectral-density difference of about 1,604.752% between 24 fungal electrode-pair records and 8 non-inoculated control records (p<0.001). The study supports a specialized laboratory measurement of fungal-associated electrical activity; it does not decode a fungal language.
limitations: This is a laboratory sensor/method study on one strain, not an animal-style communication experiment. Extracellular voltage and frequency patterns do not identify a message, receiver, referent or semantic code. For the post-induction drug/carrier comparisons, Table 1 lists n=3 and no contrast is statistically significant: cycloheximide −74.214% (p=.327), voriconazole +1,201.803% (p=.391), calcimycin +58.503% (p=.580), and sodium azide +1,358.933% (p=.116). The calcimycin pattern matched its DMSO carrier, which the authors consider likely electrode interference; the sodium-azide series also had a brief water-control anomaly. The main text does not establish whether electrode-pair counts are independent biological replicates. The 2024 critique and 2025 review describe unresolved measurement and interpretation challenges. Mendeley displays CC BY 4.0 but its visible Files section contains no file entries; no dataset files were reviewed. The article's data statement points to Method S1 for code, while its software table points to Document S2; the supplement, code bytes and component-specific terms remain unreviewed.
lesson: Treat fungal electrophysiology as a separate sensing channel that needs laboratory electrodes, environmental controls and biological controls. Evidence of stimulus-associated activity is not evidence of language or of a phone-mediated way to talk with mushrooms.

title: Do fungi have a language? What electrical recordings show
seo_description: A fungal spike paper proposed word-like patterns. Later critique and methods review explain why signals, artifacts and meaning differ.
review_depth: Reviewed the full arXiv HTML text of Adamatzky's 2021 preprint, including recording methods, event detection, grouping rules, results and discussion; checked the published 2022 Royal Society article metadata and institutional article-rights record. Reviewed the 2024 critique's publisher abstract and visible selected sections, not its full text. Reviewed the full 2025 FEMS review sections on fungal electrophysiology, macroscopic mushroom recordings, the authors' method-replication attempt, caveats and future methods, plus its article license. Inspected the official Zenodo v1 record and file metadata only. No files were downloaded, no analysis was reproduced, and no independent specialist review was received.
review_locator: Adamatzky (2021 preprint; peer-reviewed article published 2022): Methods; Table 1; spike grouping and word-length comparison; Discussion and future directions. Blatt et al. (2024): publisher abstract and visible introduction/section snippets only. Schintke et al. (2025): full article, especially Table 1, extracellular electrode caveats, mushroom recording and replication sections, and license statement. Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.5790768: v1 record, four-file inventory, checksums and Rights section.
finding: Adamatzky's peer-reviewed 2022 paper reports extracellular voltage recordings from four fungal species. It sampled one value per second from differential electrode pairs placed 1–2 cm apart, recorded up to eight pairs at once, and reports about 1.5 days for Schizophyllum commune and about five days for each other species. The analysis used species-specific thresholds to identify spikes, then grouped them into proposed “words” using one or two times each species' mean inter-spike interval. The resulting spike-count distribution was compared with human-language word lengths. This is a published pattern-analysis hypothesis, not a decoded fungal vocabulary or conversation.
limitations: The grouping threshold is an analyst-defined analogy, and similar word-length distributions do not identify a sender's message, a receiver, a referent or a semantic code. The 2024 Blatt et al. commentary argues that the language claim is premature and that non-biological voltage noise and artifacts may account for measured patterns; its full text was not accessible in this review. The 2025 FEMS review describes an attempted method replication in Pleurotus pulmonarius: it reports disturbance-associated spikes from opening the incubator, nearby footsteps and automatic window shades in both fungal and control recordings, and calls for stronger environmental shielding and measurement controls. That is a methods warning, not a definitive disproof of all fungal electrical physiology. The linked 2021 Zenodo dataset lists four archives totaling 84.6 MB, but no license was displayed in its Rights section. No archive, code or weights were acquired, and no benchmark or model was run.
lesson: Keep four questions separate: whether an electrode records a voltage; whether the voltage is biological; whether it reliably predicts a controlled physiological response; and whether a receiver uses it as information. The paper addresses the first and proposes analyses relevant to the latter questions, but does not establish a semantic language. A phone microphone cannot measure these electrical potentials.
next_review: Before any reproduction, resolve the Zenodo dataset's reuse terms and file provenance, then ask a mycologist and electrophysiologist to review a preregistered, lab-based replication. It should include independently grown cultures, colonized and sterile-medium controls, sham/reference-electrode checks, continuous environmental logs, blinded condition labels and frozen signal-processing rules. Only test a stimulus-response prediction after those measurement controls pass; no training or consumer translation feature is proposed.

title: Ice-crystal claims: why beautiful images need stronger tests
review_depth: Reviewed the full 2006 four-page article, full 2008 Journal of Scientific Exploration paper, Douglas Stokes’s 2009 letter (p. 83), and Kokubo, Nemoto and Kawano’s 2017 technical note (pp. 73–86). Checked the reported designs, outcomes and experimental units. The 2006 full text was read from an author-hosted copy; its indexed PubMed record remains linked. Raw photographs, original analysis files/code and a full systematic literature search were not reviewed; no independent specialist review was obtained.
finding: The 2006 pilot reports that 100 blind judges gave higher beauty ratings to 24 selected treated-condition images than to 16 control images (means 2.87 vs 1.88; one-tailed p=.001). The images came from just four bottles (two per condition), and only drops with a discernible crystal were photographed. The same investigator group’s 2008 triple-blind follow-up used six bottles (two per condition) and 300 drop photographs. Its authors reported a weak three-condition beauty effect (p=.03) and a treated-versus-proximal-control comparison at p=.05, one-tailed; the beauty effect was not significant after adjustment for image interest (p=.20), and the three-condition objective-contrast result was not significant (p=.25). These are reports by the study authors, not independent confirmation.
limitations: The 2006 image-level ratings do not create more independent treated water sources than the four bottles; the authors themselves noted different treatment/control environments, selective photographing of visible crystals and the need to assess all drops and use more objective measures. The 2008 authors modeled bottles as random effects but used only two bottles per condition. Stokes’s 2009 letter specifically critiques the 2008 treated-versus-proximal comparison: treating the four bottles as the units gives a maximum one-tailed exact rank probability of 1/6 (.167). This letter does not directly analyze the 2006 pilot. The 2017 technical note discusses dependent photographs and too few bottles; its authors also acknowledge their own judge-level tests were invalid and their two-bottle-per-condition trials too small. That small methods study is not a decisive independent null replication. No reviewed study shows that water understands words, carries a message, or reliably changes crystal structure because of thought.
lesson: Many photographs and ratings cannot substitute for independent experimental units. A communication claim also needs a defined sender and receiver, a signal, and a controlled functional response; visual resemblance or a human beauty score is not a message. This is a lesson in research design, not biological evidence or a basis for Talk2Nature machine learning.
next_review: Keep this as a methods-critical case only. Any new test would need specialist review, preregistration, many independently randomized bottle batches, blinded handling, all-drop measurement, objective outcomes, a frozen analysis and independent replication. Do not use these papers to train or benchmark an animal-communication model.

title: Parrot owners can contribute; species still matter
review_depth: Full main article text, including methods, results, discussion, data-availability and rights statements, reviewed through the Europe PMC full-text XML. Official Figshare v4 API metadata and its single-file manifest were checked. The supplementary questionnaire (Appendix 1), workbook, and raw responses were not inspected or acquired.
finding: The authors received 898 voluntary survey responses and retained a cleaned sample of 877 companion parrots across 33 genera and 73 species after quality checks and excluding birds not reported to mimic human sounds. Respondents said sampled parrots sometimes (36%) or frequently (53%) used mimicked vocalizations in appropriate human contexts without prompting. These are caregiver reports, not independently observed events or receiver tests.
limitations: Recruitment used email and social media with parrot advocacy, care, and interest groups and was explicitly biased toward birds that mimic human sounds. The survey asked respondents for their names and email addresses; although the published data item declares CC BY 4.0, the XLSX has not been inspected, so presence or absence of identifiers, consent scope, and privacy suitability are unknown. The contextual-use measure is owner-assessed, not a timestamped recording or controlled behavioral response. This dataset is not an acoustic corpus, decoded vocabulary, or validated training set.
lesson: A community survey can expose the kinds of context people notice, but it should not collapse caregiver interpretation into scientific labels. A Talk2Nature observation flow should preserve a time-stamped observation, the caregiver's interpretation, the source recording, and any later independent review as separate fields, with species and individual uncertainty explicit.

Seek qualified parrot-communication review of a prospective observer codebook; do not admit this owner-survey table to audio-model training.

title: When companion parrots use names: what a survey can and cannot show
seo_description: A caregiver survey reports name use across companion parrots. It suggests observation questions, not an audio corpus or proof of call meaning.
review_depth: PLOS ONE article HTML reviewed for abstract, methods, results and discussion; the official correction notice was checked. Supporting information, raw survey data and figures were not downloaded or inspected, and no independent reanalysis was performed.
finding: The survey reports on 1,202 companion parrots across 89 species; phrase-use information was supplied for 884 birds, with names reported for 413. Multiple observers identified 131 reported examples of appropriate name use across 88 birds and 30 species, and 69 individualized examples across 42 birds and 19 species.
limitations: These are human survey reports about learned human-language phrases, not recordings or experiments on natural parrot calls. Context was supplied or interpreted by respondents, reports were not representative, and the authors state that scoring remained subjective and does not unequivocally demonstrate understanding. The abstract says 802 example phrases contained names while the Results section says 801; the May 2026 correction adds ORCID identifiers only. Methods say the survey requested both respondent and parrot names. The article describes its S2 phrase dataset as de-identified, but we have not inspected that workbook or independently assessed disclosure risk; review the exact files and terms before reuse.
lesson: For a simple phone workflow, keep three things distinct: a time-stamped event someone could observe, the owner's own description of context, and any later scientific interpretation. Use aliases, preserve unknowns, and never turn an owner's interpretation into a model label by default. This survey is useful for designing a participatory observation interface, not for training an audio model or claiming that parrots translate human speech.
next_review: Compare the survey's categories with controlled parrot name-use studies and ask a qualified parrot-communication researcher to review a prospective, privacy-preserving codebook before any participant data collection. A useful follow-up would test observer agreement on directly observed context separately from owner-reported interpretation.

title: Budgerigar vocal signatures: caller identity, not call meaning
seo_description: A lab study identified known budgerigar callers from contact calls; the split design does not show call meaning or unseen-bird performance.
kind: Neural and bioacoustic study with a separate data deposit
review_depth: Reviewed the full Current Biology article text through NCBI PMC E-utilities (PMCID PMC10799565), including call-elicitation, VAE/SVM methods, results, discussion, animal-care and data/code statements. Rechecked the version-1 Mendeley landing-page description and API documentation against the prior checksum-pinned one-file inspection. No new data files were acquired or parsed; no code/model was run, no reanalysis or independent review was performed.
review_locator: PMC full text: Results sections on call elicitation, VAE-based caller identity, vocal change over time, AFP-inactivated receiver responses, call structure and individual discriminability; STAR Methods sections on study participants, contact-call playback, pharmacological inactivation, VAE, SVM and data/code availability. Mendeley v1 landing page: raw MATLAB struct-array data, Figure 2 in ColonyNoiseCalls, Figures 3–5 in acoustiSAT_MAO.mat; API access boundary documented separately.
finding: The full article used 16 adult budgerigars, with eight in the contact-call cohort and five in the neural-inactivation experiment. Playback of colony-noise segments elicited 180–1,612 contact calls per bird per day in the eight-bird cohort. A VAE representation and SVM identified callers at over 90% accuracy in a balanced random 80/20 call-level split, repeated 50 times; accuracy remained about 90% for two shared call types. A classifier trained at week 3 and tested at week 15 fell from about 90% to 40%, consistent with call change over time. In the separate five-bird experiment, birds still responded to individual calls during AFP inactivation, although response rate fell in three birds and latency effects varied. Inactivation altered call acoustics and reduced individual discriminability. These are bounded acoustic identity and production findings, not decoded meaning.
limitations: The reported identity classifier randomly split calls from the same known birds; no held-out-bird test is reported, so its accuracy is not generalization to unseen animals, species, sites or devices. The study used small captive groups, controlled loudspeaker playback, directional laboratory microphones and invasive neural interventions. Receiver responses were measured in five birds and were not a test of name comprehension or call meaning. The official data page associates ColonyNoiseCalls with Figure 2, the eight-bird contact-call identity analysis; the single inspected file has no verified mapping to a specific bird, session or condition and no independent behavior-label field. The paper's reviewed methods do not state a digitization rate, so the sample's stored 44,101 value remains unexplained. The dataset separately declares CC BY 4.0; custom scripts are available from the lead contact without a verified public license.
lesson: Treat caller identity, receiver response, context association and communicative meaning as different outcomes. A first identity benchmark would need bird-grouped holdouts; a meaning claim would need independently measured receiver behavior. The specialized playback and neural methods do not validate a phone workflow or justify app playback.
next_review: If the deposit is considered for a defined analysis, obtain the versioned per-file manifest and map this sample to caller, session and condition; resolve the sample rate against acquisition metadata rather than guessing from the filename. The official file-list API requires OAuth2 and the unauthenticated request returned 401. Verify exact file terms and obtain independent avian-bioacoustics/statistical review before any benchmark. Until then, keep this study as a methods comparator, not a ready context or translation benchmark.

title: What parrot touchscreen research can—and cannot—tell us
seo_description: A full review of a CHI 2024 parrot touchscreen study: ergonomics and welfare insights, with limits on animal-facing apps.
review_depth: On October 14, reviewed the full article text from the 16-page published PDF hosted by the University of Glasgow, from the abstract through the conclusion, including the caregiver survey/pilot, participant criteria, ethics, protocol, data cleaning, results, limitations and design guidelines. Figures were not visually reanalyzed; no raw data, code, supplements or independent analysis were available or inspected.
finding: In the study's specific 10.1-inch tablet task, 17 trained pet parrots completed 4,720 selected target touches (8,995 counting follow-on taps). Hit rate increased with target width from 19.29% at 40 dp to 47.08% at 130 dp; the study found no significant effect of target distance and no detected difference in touch-point precision by target width. The authors' 300 ms rule classified 45.73% of taps as multi-taps. This is touchscreen-ergonomics evidence, not a communication test.
limitations: Twenty adult home-kept parrots entered and 17 completed testing after gradual training; eligibility required prior comfort with screens/objects and balloon-pop-style games, and caregivers needed animal-training experience and time. Two birds did not reach stable engagement within six weeks and one showed slight aggression. Testing used a 10.1-inch Galaxy Tab A at a fixed angle and size-specific perch distances, not phones or an ordinary untrained interaction. Hit-rate differences may reflect larger target area, not improved precision; the exact-width comparison found no precision difference. The proposed touch-and-retreat account is an interpretation of video observations, not a separately quantified mechanism. Caregiver survey responses are self-report. The University of Glasgow record lists CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 and 'Data Availability Statement: No'; raw data and a separate code license were not established. No independent specialist review or replication has been completed.
lesson: Keep the current Field Companion human-operated and passive. A future parrot-operated enrichment interface would be a separate animal-computer-interaction project requiring qualified avian/ACI and welfare review, individual and species-aware testing, a voluntary exit, short flexible sessions and caregiver support. The 100–130 dp target range is specific to this tablet/perch setup and must not be treated as a phone or universal species specification. Do not infer preference, comprehension, call meaning or communication from a touch; this paper is not an acoustic ML dataset and does not justify adding playback to the current app.
next_review: Seek independent avian and animal-computer-interaction review of the study's design implications and welfare requirements. Check for a later correction or newly released data/code record before any reuse; contact authors only with separate authorization. Do not prototype an animal-operated interface without an approved welfare protocol, hardware-specific feasibility work and a safe voluntary-exit design.

A 10.1-inch Galaxy Tab A was set at a 70-degree angle on a stand in the bird's familiar home setting. Perch distance varied by bird-size category; this was a tablet study, not a phone test.

A 12-caregiver survey and five-bird pilot informed a three-month study. Gradual training lasted up to six weeks. Caregivers limited work to at most three sessions per day and 30 minutes per day; the 17 completers were those who reached stable engagement.

A custom Fitts-style app presented five series of five targets, split into 5–15 tasks at a time according to interest and fatigue. Birds had an exit button and a clear route away; caregivers were trained to stop on distress, and a parrot behaviorist reviewed sessions.

The app recorded target hits, movement time and touch positions; video review covered on-task behavior. Two researchers independently coded distracted versus on-task segments, with 97% reported agreement.

Across 892 series, hit rate rose from 19.29% at 40 dp to 47.08% at 130 dp, while target distance was not significant and touch-point precision did not differ by target width. The study's 300 ms rule classified 45.73% as multi-taps. A larger touch target improved hit rate in this setup; it did not establish a universal 100–130 dp phone requirement.

The authors propose a touch-and-retreat explanation for low Fitts-law fit based on video observations; this behavior was not separately quantified. A caregiver survey and perceived enrichment are not independent measures of animal preference or communication.

Its vocalization-level cross-validation does not establish generalization to held-out bats. The 2023 follow-up used sequences from three adult females; the context HMM used 326 sequences (2,953 syllables), formed 12,900 n-grams and reported overall balanced accuracy 66 ± 10 under random eight-fold cross-validation. Shuffling syllable order left the score unchanged. These are predictions of observer-coded context, not evidence that bats or humans interpret a call as a message. The 2023 authors say behavioral experiments are needed to establish biological relevance. The laboratory archive used synchronized video, isolated chambers and specialized 250 kHz ultrasound recording; ordinary phone recordings cannot be assumed to match its bandwidth, calibration or capture conditions. The Figshare public item API declares CC0 1.0 for archive item 4556074 and lists one 3,049,199,327-byte ZIP; its payload and embedded rights notices were not inspected. The separate annotation item 4555903 declares CC0 1.0; its 3,286,405-byte file was locally size/MD5 verified. The aggregate audit found 91,080 rows, 87,986 distinct file IDs, no malformed fields and exact Table 4 count matches. These are structural/transcription checks, not independent validation. title: Wild parrot duet structure: sequence patterns, not decoded meaning
seo_description: Wild yellow-naped amazons show flexible duet sequences, but the study could not confidently assign meanings to calls or duets.
kind: Wild vocal-sequence study and dataset review
review_stage: Targeted primary article, dataset metadata and reuse-rights review
review_depth: Reviewed the publisher article HTML for its abstract, sites and recordings, call categorization, acoustic analyses, syntax methods and results, discussion, data-availability statement and supplementary-file inventory. Reviewed the full Dryad dataset landing page and README description and Dryad’s current reuse-rights guide. The workbook and publisher supplements were not downloaded or inspected; no published analysis was reproduced.
finding: The study examined warble duets from 13 mated pairs of wild yellow-naped amazons in north-west Costa Rica during 2006–2008. The authors report creating 1,136 duet files; 52 high-quality warble duets from 12 pairs were used in the syntax analysis. They report recurring call types, flexible ordering, 19 positive and four negative call-type associations, while most complete duet sequences were unique. This is evidence of measurable sequence structure in this study, not a translated conversation.
limitations: Analysis-specific sample counts differ: the initial lexicon is described as 469 calls from 54 duets and 13 pairs, while syntax analysis used 52 duets from 12 pairs. Methods describe 36 multi-example call types plus 11 one-time forms grouped as “Unknown”; results report 36 call types and three variants. The reported 92% repeatability came from two supervised undergraduate scorers scoring 15 hidden duets three times; it is not independent external validation. Calls could overlap and be difficult to segment, and sex assignment relied on established duet-order rules. Quadratic discriminant analysis and naive Bayes did not classify the full call-type set; pairwise naive Bayes separated only two similar types. Syntax/collocation is not semantic decoding: the authors state that they cannot confidently assign meanings to calls, collocates or duets and discuss possible territory-defense functions. Recordings used a tripod-mounted directional microphone and video, not ordinary phone capture. The species is described as Critically Endangered, so this atlas uses country-scale geography only. Dryad lists a small measurements workbook, not raw audio; the publisher separately lists a WAV and two DOCX supplements whose terms and contents were not reviewed. The specific article reuse license was not established. No Talk2Nature specialist review, independent replication or model result exists.
lesson: For Talk2Nature, represent pair or individual identity, ordered event positions, timing, overlap, uncertain caller identity and annotation provenance separately. Preserve “unknown” and distinguish a next vocal event from a response. Keep sequence structure, context association and experimentally demonstrated meaning as different evidence levels. This wild-species study is a methods comparator; it does not establish that household phone recordings are suitable or change the provisional companion-parrot pilot.

Before considering the workbook, review the exact rows and pair identifiers under a specialist-led sensitive-species and research-use assessment; evaluate article and supplementary-file terms separately. title: A parrot can imitate a call to address another bird. What the experiment shows.
seo_description: A controlled conure study links targeted call imitation to receiver responses; it does not establish human-like translation or justify app playback.
taxon: Orange-fronted conure (Eupsittula canicularis; the 2012 paper uses Aratinga canicularis)
review_stage: Full-text methods and results review
review_depth: Reviewed the full primary PLOS article text for the abstract, introduction, Materials and Methods, Results, Discussion, Ethics Statement and article license. finding: Balsby, Momberg and Dabelsteen tested whether a call resembling one of two paired birds would selectively affect that bird. They studied 36 temporarily captive wild conures from 27 flocks. After exclusions, 44 of 72 trial periods were analyzed. Targeted birds responded with higher call rates and shorter latency overall, while some non-target responses were also recorded. The authors interpret this as evidence that vocal imitation can address a specific individual in this species and setting.
study_snapshot: 36 wild-caught orange-fronted conures from 27 flocks, placed in 18 pairs in outdoor aviaries for a short-term study.
A recorded contact-call loop was selected to resemble one of the two birds; each pair received four randomized trials.
Audio and video were used to count calls, estimate response latency and identify callers across the small social network.
44 of 72 trial periods were retained after exclusions for uncertain caller identity or outside-bird interactions.
The paper reports following Animal Behaviour Society guidelines and holding local research and CITES permits.
expert_review: This Talk2Nature synthesis has not received independent review by an avian communication specialist.
limitations: This was a controlled playback study of 36 wild-caught orange-fronted conures from 27 flocks, paired in short-term outdoor aviaries during 2007. Of 72 trial periods, 44 were retained for analysis after caller-assignment and outside-interaction exclusions. The authors report higher call rates and shorter response latency for the targeted bird overall, with a sex-specific call-rate pattern; non-target birds also responded. This supports a bounded, context-specific receiver response to acoustically targeted imitation, not decoding of sentence meaning, general conversation, or a result transferable to pet parrots, other species or phone speakers. The experiment used captured birds, repeated playback and video observation under research permits. No Talk2Nature replication or independent specialist review exists.
lesson: A receiver response can support a narrow claim about signal function in a defined context without revealing semantic content. The study also shows why a focal bird cannot always be analyzed alone: non-target flock members may respond. For our app, playback is an intervention, not a harmless conversational interface. Keep public tools passive; any later playback experiment needs qualified scientific and animal-welfare review, a defined protocol and relevant permits.

Their three-fold evaluation describes subject-independent development/test partitions with class balance. Across pooled test predictions, they report unweighted average recall of 22.4% for an SVM using ten pitch features, 27.7% for ResNet-50 and 33.3% for EfficientNet-B0. The paper says EfficientNet used ImageNet-pretrained initialization and promises to release code and partitions upon acceptance. The first author’s linked GitHub account lists 13 public repositories, with no matching paper repository visible in the checked list. The separately reviewed Earth Species Library notebooks are pinned to a 2021 commit, before the EUSIPCO paper: its 02 notebook predicts emitter identity and uses a shuffled, row-level stratified five-fold split; 99a documents archive preprocessing but says a train/validation split is not apparent and creates none; 99b makes a reduced emitter-identity subset. These notebooks do not reproduce the later paper or verify its folds. The EUSIPCO result predicts video-coded interaction context in captive bats; it does not test message meaning or receiver comprehension. An aggregate-only audit of the full 91,080-row annotation component (not the paper’s 35,074-record filtered set) found 48 known IDs across the two role columns and 70,001 rows with two identified participants. This is a description of the source table, not verification of the paper’s split or model results. review_request.summary: We invite a qualified bat bioacoustics or animal-behavior researcher to assess the generalization claim and the minimum evidence needed to audit it. What evidence is needed to verify that all relevant participant roles and repeated recordings are isolated across the reported development/test folds? Which dates, channels, treatments, chambers or recording sessions could confound generalization?
Are context-only, class-prior, recording-channel/background and shuffled-label baselines adequate for this question? What uncertainty estimate respects repeated animals, pairs and sessions?
What is the smallest lawful, technically sound metadata check that could resolve the key uncertainty? Is the separate FileInfo.csv actually necessary, given its size and missing upstream checksum?

limitations: The paper’s subject-independent test split is a positive reported safeguard, but Talk2Nature has not inspected the partitions or verified which identities, roles, sessions, dates, microphones, chambers or treatments cross folds. The training/validation split inside each development set ignores identity. Confidence intervals bootstrap individual predictions rather than clustered animals or sessions. Class frequencies are unequal and grooming recall is zero. Context is an observer-coded group/action category, not a test of receiver interpretation. The 2026-10-23 public-code search covered the first author’s 13-repository owner inventory and an exact-title GitHub repository search, not coauthor/lab/archive locations; a Zenodo API search was inaccessible and yielded no negative finding. The pinned Earth Species notebook snapshot predates the EUSIPCO paper and therefore is not its promised release; a separate coauthor/lab/archive release may still exist. The repository root inventory has no visible LICENSE, and notebook 99a states code license “to be linked”; it declares dataset CC BY 4.0, which is not reconciled with Talk2Nature’s direct item-level Figshare records or derived archive-copy provenance. No independent reproduction or specialist review exists. The paper reports ImageNet-pretrained vision weights, not a bioacoustic foundation model. The arXiv v1 manuscript declares CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; proceedings-copy reuse terms were not separately reviewed. The identity graph covers the complete annotation table, not the 35,074 records used by the 2024 paper, and cannot establish whether its three folds isolate all interacting bats, emitters only, sessions, channels, treatments or chamber backgrounds. Metadata.pdf provides treatment and subject context, but the necessary per-file timestamp/channel join is in a separate 31,574,701-byte FileInfo.csv item with no upstream MD5; it was not fetched. The aggregate graph is not an independent split or leakage test. The 2026-10-23 filtered subset audit reproduces the published row count, not the authors' exact selected-row manifest. Under source-FileID plus positive-known-participant grouping, nine components remain and the largest contains 95.56% of the filtered annotations; a balanced 70/15/15 whole-group split cannot be made without dividing that component. This does not establish what split the paper used. Unknown participant roles may hide more links, and the available annotation table does not resolve session, date, channel, treatment or chamber grouping. No model was run.

The Earth Species loader’s shuffled row-level split evaluates emitter identity rather than unseen-animal context prediction; the mini archive drops context labels. Source tables make those checks possible in principle but do not prove the reported folds. title: BioCPPNet separates overlapping calls—it does not decode them

taxon: Rhesus macaque, bottlenose dolphin and Egyptian fruit bat

finding: BioCPPNet is a supervised source-separation pipeline, an audio-cleanup step rather than a communication decoder. The study constructs mixtures by additively combining known individual vocalizations, then trains a lightweight U-Net to estimate separated waveforms. It evaluates macaque, dolphin and Egyptian-fruit-bat material. For bats, the paper reports 31,399 calls from 15 highly represented individuals, with 12 used in a closed-speaker regime and three held for an open-speaker evaluation. It reports bat validation SI-SDR 9.7 and downstream caller-identity accuracy 57.5% for the closed-speaker setting; the open-speaker SI-SDR is reported as 10.0. Those results concern reconstruction and identity on generated mixtures, not behavior, context meaning, receiver comprehension or conversation.
study_snapshot: Separate two or three overlapping animal-call streams into estimated source waveforms.
The paper synthetically adds individually annotated vocalizations or vocalization streams to create mixtures with known source waveforms.

The reported bat material uses calls from 15 individuals: 12 for the closed-speaker regime and three for the open-speaker test. The model is evaluated with SI-SDR and a downstream individual-identity classifier.

The paper links macaque and Egyptian-fruit-bat datasets; dolphin recordings were provided under license and are not public. Article terms are CC BY 4.0, while implementation-code terms were not visible in the reviewed repository root.
expert_review: This Talk2Nature synthesis has not received independent review by a bioacoustic source-separation specialist.
limitations: The mixtures are constructed from known isolated source recordings, so the reported experiment does not by itself validate performance on naturally recorded, uncontrolled field mixtures. SI-SDR and caller-identity accuracy are reconstruction proxies, not evidence that a model identified call purpose or meaning. The bat open-speaker test uses three held-out individuals from the selected subset, and Talk2Nature has not reproduced the pipeline or audited source/session overlap. The repository has no visible LICENSE at the reviewed commit, so implementation reuse is not cleared. Dataset, source audio, generated mixtures, model weights and paper terms remain separate; dolphin data are explicitly restricted. No independent reproduction or expert review exists.
lesson: Keep the analysis stages distinct: detection, overlap separation, caller/source attribution, observable context association, and experimentally supported receiver response answer different questions. Source separation could make later observation or annotation more usable, but it cannot turn an acoustic stream into a translated sentence. Any future Talk2Nature separation module needs licensed inputs, known-source synthetic fixtures, a rights-cleared model/code path and evaluation against natural field recordings before public claims.
next_review: Ask a qualified bioacoustics reviewer whether source separation addresses a real bottleneck in the project's selected species and phone-recording workflow. Before implementation reuse, verify the exact repository license and inspect code/data/model provenance under a bounded, non-installing review. If pursued, first define a rights-cleared synthetic-mixture evaluation with source checksums, fixed splits, SI-SDR plus downstream utility and failure cases; this technical rehearsal must remain separate from any semantic-communication claim. Keep AutoResearch NOT READY until all benchmark gates are met.

title: Can trees talk through fungi? What mycorrhizal networks show

Karst, Jones and Hoeksema (2023) warn that popular and scientific claims about widespread forest networks and beneficial “mother tree” transfers can outrun the evidence and report positive citation bias. Henriksson et al. (2023) argue that isotope studies do not yet establish significant net carbon transfer through these networks that benefits recipients, and discuss alternative pathways. Simard, Ryan and Perry (2025) respond that multiple methods support network connections and context-dependent transfer in forests. This published disagreement is a reason to state the evidence level precisely, not to declare either that networks never occur or that trees have a demonstrated shared language.
limitations: This debate is especially about forest ecology and ectomycorrhizal systems; it does not settle every plant–fungus relationship. A fungal connection or isotope transfer is not by itself evidence that one plant sent information another received. The 2025 response is explicitly an Opinion by researchers involved in this field, not an independent replication. One author of the 2023 New Phytologist review disclosed a financial interest in an organic-fertilizer company. The linked primary studies and their methods were not exhaustively reviewed here.
lesson: Keep the claims on separate rungs: demonstrate the fungal connection; trace the material and route; measure an independent receiver response; test whether a sender-derived signal explains that response better than soil, water, root, stress or other pathways. The paper states that samples from one recording stay in only one split, with a default 70/15/15 train/validation/test split; it does not establish individual-animal holdout. Also reviewed the official repository split guide, Edmond V2.0 metadata and access guidance, and current Edmond Terms of Use on October 14, 2026. The terms' MPS-associated service wording does not explicitly clarify its application to external downloaders of existing public datasets. The supplement's split tables, exact V2 archive manifest and individual/session recurrence remain unreviewed. No data, code or model was acquired or run; no terms were accepted and metrics were not reproduced.

Its paper reports recording-level partitioning (samples from a recording stay within one split) and a default 70/15/15 train/validation/test split. For target/noise detection, it reports mean test-set accuracy of 97.9% (range 94.5–99.8%) and, separately, an average AUC of 95.9% (range 91.7–99.1%) across 33 additional unseen animal-specific recordings. In a separate monk-parakeet task, the paper reports 92.7% call-type accuracy on human-labeled test samples and 88.4% on detector-selected segments. These are upstream-reported results, not Talk2Nature measurements; acoustic class prediction does not establish behavior, receiver comprehension or meaning.
limitations: The recording-level split supports a held-out-recording interpretation, but the article does not state that individual animals are held out; the repository's YEAR+TAPENAME grouping guidance also does not prove individual separation. Edmond metadata lists a public 522.0 MB V2.0 archive, but its internal contents and split files remain unreviewed, and the deposit is described as target/noise data rather than the paper's separate call-type corpus. Edmond's public-data guide says downloads require acceptance of its terms and the dataset license. The current Terms of Use gives an MPS-associated research-service restriction but does not separately explain its application to external downloaders of existing public datasets; no terms were accepted. The manuscript reports strong EDANSA-2019 test performance but a marked drop on the different BEsound recording domain, especially for human and geophysical sounds. Its best BEsound macro-F1 of 0.799 applies class-specific thresholds and window-count settings selected on BEsound itself; it should be treated as a tuned evaluation result rather than an untouched holdout estimate. The ecological case study uses model predictions to pre-filter audio before calculating conventional acoustic indices. This can help characterize recording context, but it does not say which species vocalized or what a call means. The paper uses public EDANSA together with BEsound and other collections that are not all directly accessible. Code, weights, article and data have distinct licenses: the pinned training repository declares MIT, the Hub model declares CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, the arXiv paper declares CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, and Zenodo's API declares CC BY 4.0 for the EDANSA record while the rendered license field is blank.

Domain, recorder and annotation differences matter; reported errors include insect sounds confused with biophony, wind/background noise around silence/geophony, and masking when classes co-occur. Some training collections are private or available only on request. The code repository is marked under construction. Model weight reuse is non-commercial under its declared CC BY-NC-SA terms; underlying encoder, dependencies and all dataset components need separate review. No Talk2Nature result is reproduced.

Keep any eventual app context optional, human-reviewed and multi-label; preserve co-occurrence and unknowns, and do not silently convert broad soundscape predictions into a focal animal identity or behavioral explanation. title: WhAM: acoustic style transfer is not whale translation
seo_description: WhAM generates sperm-whale-style audio and learns features for coda classification. Its acoustic style transfer does not translate whale meaning.

finding: WhAM fine-tunes the music-pretrained VampNet masked acoustic token model in two stages: domain adaptation on animal-audio collections, then sperm-whale-specific training on DSWP and CETI. The paper describes 2,507 DSWP and 7,653 CETI annotated codas for this work. It evaluates generated audio with Fréchet Audio Distance and a five-expert listening study, and tests learned embeddings on coda detection, rhythm, social-unit and vowel-type classification. The paper explicitly defines “translation” as converting prompts, including noise or other animal sounds, into sperm-whale coda-like acoustic style; it says semantic translation remains a separate, more ambitious goal. On the reported classification table, WhAM exceeds simple random/majority baselines but the reported specialist or general bioacoustic embeddings perform better across these tasks. For example, social-unit accuracy is 70.5% for WhAM versus 93.2% for BirdNET. The paper describes social-unit classification within data from a single vocal clan as closer to speaker identification than dialect classification.

The reviewed description does not establish a separate validation set or grouping by whale, recording, session or source, so the reported test metrics should not be treated as an untouched independent estimate. The public DSWP card currently lists 1,501 isolated snippets (~45 minutes; 585 MB), fewer than the paper’s 2,507 DSWP training codas; the exact relationship is unresolved. The card says the clips lack behavioral context and per-file recording-system metadata and all come from one clan and region. The paper identifies codec limitations, unnatural synthetic click onset/decay/background, echolocation-like artifacts and possible echolocation contamination in data prepared as communication codas. The acoustic outputs and classification labels do not demonstrate receiver comprehension, behavioral function or meaning. The paper is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, code MIT, DSWP card CC BY 4.0, while the weight record displays no license; these are distinct component rights. No independent reproduction or specialist review occurred.

title: How great tits respond to a distant species’ mobbing calls
seo_description: A 2025 playback study tests great-tit responses to Carolina wren mobbing calls, with limits on what receiver behavior proves about meaning.
review_stage: Publisher-indexed methods/results and institutional abstract reviewed; no article file, data, or independent specialist review
review_depth: Reviewed the publisher-indexed Methods, Results and Discussion passages and the University of Western Australia repository abstract and publication/license metadata. The publisher states 96 wild great tits, six playback treatments with 16 birds each, and a single playback per bird. The indexed text exposes stimulus construction and behavioral outcomes; direct ScienceDirect retrieval returned HTTP 403, so figures, supplements, full statistical details, and article-level context were not reviewed.
finding: Great tits approached the loudspeaker more often during call playbacks than during control playbacks, but approach did not significantly differ among call treatments. Wing-flicking was more likely after the complete two-part call sequence (labelled FME–D by the authors) than after D-only calls or controls for both great-tit and Carolina-wren stimuli. The authors note that the alert/recruitment functions of the Carolina wren's FME and D parts were not confirmed. It did not include reversed-order Carolina-wren sequences, so it does not isolate call order as the cause. Carolina-wren stimuli came from four recorded individuals but were reduced to two constructed tracks per call treatment; the authors note that more stimulus diversity would be ideal. Similar behavior can reflect response to a mobbing-like acoustic pattern without demonstrating a shared semantic representation or receiver translation. No Talk2Nature model or app feature was tested.

To test how a sequence is decoded, compare sequence and component calls, reverse order, control acoustic similarity and novelty, use diverse independent callers, and predefine a receiver-side behavioral measure. Cross-species response is a hypothesis-generating bridge, not evidence of unrestricted shared language.

75 hours of non-continuous recordings made at about 30 m with directional microphones and solid-state recorders; 44.1 or 48 kHz WAV, with 48 kHz material resampled to 44.1 kHz.
Nesting, threat, alarm, foraging, perched, take-off, flight, landing and food soliciting. The study is observational; it did not test playback responses.

Researchers classified 8,622 notes into 152 note-types. Acoustic-parameter analyses used 58 types meeting frequency and recording-quality criteria; the note-type pDFA used 28 types emitted by more than one individual.

Publisher lists a 116 kB XLSX of statistical-analysis data, context descriptions, a note-frequency table and sound examples. The article notes low sample sizes in some contexts and says playback evidence is needed to establish signal function. GLMM analyses excluded food soliciting; the pDFA classifies note types, not behavioral contexts, and its permutation comparison is not an untouched held-out-animal test. Some off-nest individual identities were inferred from day and distance. The paper does not report quantified independent context-label agreement. Supplement descriptions conflict with several linked file extensions; no data or example audio was opened, and the listed files do not describe a full 75-hour archive. The acoustic setup and wild species do not validate ordinary phone capture or household-parrot behavior.
lesson: Keep the observation, acoustic event, behavioral context and interpretation as separate records. A call can be associated with multiple contexts, and a note-type classification result is not a behavior prediction or translation. Use this paper to design labels and confound checks, not as evidence that Talk2Nature can infer a call's meaning.

title: Phones can record wildlife, but they are not interchangeable sensors
seo_description: Nightingale and bat field studies show where smartphone recordings can help—and why microphone models, call ranges and field validation matter.
taxon: Multiple taxa: common nightingale and bats

review_depth: For Jäckel et al. (2021), reviewed the PLOS paper's methods, citizen-recording quality results, device playback comparison, discussion, rights and Zenodo data statement; the cited Zenodo deposit remains unreviewed. For Gili et al. (2024), reviewed the full publisher article and the March 13, 2024 Dryad record, visible file list and embedded README structure, as well as Dryad's CC0 and responsible-sharing policies. The separate README download returned HTTP 403. No audio archive, article supplement or code was acquired or reproduced, and no independent specialist review was completed.
finding: Two different studies show that smartphones can support bounded wildlife-acoustic tasks, but they do not create a uniform sensor. Jäckel et al. compared 5,679 Berlin citizen-science nightingale recordings with expert recordings: 53% of citizen recordings were categorized as complete songs versus 100% of expert recordings, and signal-to-noise ratios were lower for citizen recordings. In a small controlled playback comparison, estimated frequency limits varied by device. The authors nevertheless considered the citizen recordings useful for questions based on relative song-type occurrence, while cautioning about exact acoustic measurements. Gili et al. tested built-in microphones for selected 8–24 kHz bat calls. Their field/pilot work covered 35 phone models and nine bat species, but found device-model variation, occasional aliasing and loss of calls near the upper detection limit; the authors recommend preliminary detectability checks and expert verification of at least some identifications.
limitations: These studies cover different species, frequency ranges, devices, apps, protocols and outcomes; their results cannot be pooled into a general phone-quality score. The nightingale work is a Berlin project and its controlled device set was small. The bat work focuses on selected calls within 8–24 kHz at Italian and Spanish sites; it does not establish general ultrasonic capture above that range. Neither study validates current phones, current operating systems, browser capture or Talk2Nature's exact audio path. Acoustic recording or species-level detection does not demonstrate receiver comprehension or call meaning.
lesson: Keep the phone as an accessible observation tool, but treat device and capture path as part of the measurement. A browser level check is not microphone calibration, and a WAV export does not make recordings comparable across phones. Any later scientific protocol should test the chosen phone models and app path against a reference recorder for the target species and frequency range, then preserve the untouched source and protocol metadata. Collect only the minimum device information needed, with consent; do not fingerprint participants. Keep detection, identification, behavior association and meaning as separate claims.
